AB-03.c01: Knowing the parts (AB-01) and inspection (AB-02) is only half the job; you must also **use** air brakes the right way.
Using air brakes covers **normal stops**, ABS stops, **emergency stops**, stopping distance, avoiding **brake fade** on hills, and parking.
AB-03.c02: Push the brake pedal down and **control the pressure** for a smooth, safe stop.
With a manual transmission, don't push in the clutch until engine rpm is **down close to idle**.
AB-03.c03: Without ABS, locked **steering wheels** mean lost steering; other locked wheels can cause a skid, **jackknife** or spin.
ABS senses a wheel about to lock and **lowers brake pressure**; you may or may not stop faster, but you can **steer** while braking.
ABS on the tractor only, trailer only or even **1 axle** still gives more control; brake the way you always have, using only the force needed.
Only if you **always** drive a vehicle with working ABS on **all axles** may you fully apply the brakes in an emergency stop.
If ABS fails you **still have regular brakes**; drive normally and get it serviced soon.
AB-03.c04: In an emergency stop, brake so the vehicle stays in a **straight line** and you can still turn.
**Controlled braking**: brake as hard as you can without locking the wheels, with very small steering moves; release if wheels lock, then reapply.
**Stab braking**: brake all the way, release when wheels lock, and brake fully again once they start rolling.
Wheels can take **up to 1 second** to start rolling; reapply sooner and the vehicle **won't straighten out**.
AB-03.c05: **Brake lag** is the time air takes to flow through the lines: **½ second or more**; hydraulic brakes work instantly.
With air brakes, stopping distance has **4 parts**: perception + reaction + brake lag + braking distance.
At 55 mph brake lag adds about **32 feet**; the total is **over 450 feet** (142 + 61 + 32 + 216 = 451).
Figure 5.6 totals: 15 mph **81 ft**, 25 mph 155 ft, 35 mph 243 ft, 45 mph **346 ft**.
AB-03.c06: Too much heat from **overusing the brakes** instead of engine braking can make them fade or fail.
Heat causes **chemical changes in the lining** that reduce friction and makes the **drums expand**, so shoes press with less force.
Brakes **out of adjustment** stop doing their share first, so the others overheat and fade.
Brakes can go out of adjustment quickly, especially when hot, so **check adjustment often**.
AB-03.c07: On a long or steep downgrade, brakes are **only a supplement** to engine braking; first get into the **correct low gear**.
Brake just hard enough for a definite slowdown; release at about **5 mph below** your "safe" speed, an application of about **3 seconds**.
When speed climbs back to the safe speed, repeat; e.g. safe speed **40 mph** → brake to **35 mph**, release, repeat.
AB-03.c08: If the low-air warning comes on, **stop and safely park as soon as possible**; there may be an air leak.
Controlled braking works only while **enough air** remains; spring brakes come on at **20–45 psi**.
Spring brakes **don't work on all axles**, so a heavy vehicle takes a long distance to stop; a light load or slippery road can mean an uncontrolled skid.
It is much safer to stop while you still have air for the **foot brake**.
AB-03.c09: Use the parking brakes whenever you park: **pull** out to apply; newer = **yellow diamond** knob, older may be a round blue knob or lever.
Don't use them when brakes are **very hot** (they can be damaged) or **very wet in freezing** temperatures (they can freeze); **chock the wheels** on level ground instead.
Dry wet brakes by **braking lightly** while driving in a low gear.
Without automatic drains, drain the tanks **at the end of every working day**; never leave the vehicle unattended without parking brakes or chocks.
